Oh, absolutely. If I try to just sit, it's like... well, it's like everything will just completely fall apart if I stop. Well, yes, I suppose it has gotten to be quite a problem. My daughter actually had to take over all my bills and paperwork last month because things were just getting so messy. Wait, what was the question? Oh, my responsibilities. Yes, it's been hard. The ladies at the church and the folks at the community garden have had to scramble to cover for me or redo plans because I just drop the ball. I feel just awful about it, really embarrassed. These are groups I care so much about, and it breaks my heart that they feel like they can't count on me anymore.

Rituals? Like... having to do things a certain way to feel better? No, I wouldn't say I do anything like that. I don't have little routines I have to follow or anything. 

Well, I mean, I do have a morning routine, but everyone has that, right? I always make my coffee first thing. I use this little French press I found at a yard sale last summer. I just can't imagine wearing jeans to an office. When I worked at the bank right after high school, we had a very strict dress code. ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Oh, my relationships... well, yes, I suppose it is. It's not just the bouncing around, it's... it's all of it. My family, they've had to step in and take over my bills and my paperwork because I just couldn't keep track of it all. It's so embarrassing. 

And the people at church, too. I used to help organize the Sunday school materials, but I kept misplacing the lesson plans or forgetting to order the right crayons. They use those big, thick crayons for the little ones, the ones that are supposed to be washable. Washable! Ha! My daughter got ahold of a red one when she was three and colored all over the living room wall. We had this terrible floral wallpaper back then, pink roses with green vines. I spent a whole afternoon scrubbing at it with soapy water, but that red wax just smeared everywhere. We ended up having to paint over the whole room. We chose a nice soft yellow. Yellow is such a happy color, don't you think? Like sunshine. I have a patch of yellow daffodils in my garden that come up every spring. They're the first things to bloom, even before the tulips. I love tulips, but the squirrels always dig up the bulbs. They're such menaces, those squirrels. I tried sprinkling cayenne pepper on the soil, but they just dug right through it...

Oh, goodness, I've done it again. I'm sorry, doctor. What was I saying? Oh, right, the church and the garden club. Yes, they've had to redo plans and cover things I've dropped. I feel awful about it. The groups I care about the most... they just don't feel they can count on me anymore. It's a terrible feeling.

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Well, yes, it definitely causes problems because I just can't seem to stop. Most days, I move from the garden, straight over to the senior center, then I'm off doing church errands, and then I come home and immediately start sorting papers on the dining table. It's like I don't take a real breath the entire day. 

Speaking of papers, I was sorting through this big stack of mail yesterday and found a catalog for gardening supplies. They had these gorgeous ceramic birdbaths. I've always wanted a birdbath in the front yard, right near the hydrangeas. Hydrangeas are so particular, though. You have to change the acidity of the soil if you want them to be blue instead of pink. My neighbor, Mr. Henderson, he has the most beautiful blue hydrangeas. He puts coffee grounds in his soil. He drinks that dark roast coffee, the kind that smells a bit burnt to me. I prefer a light breakfast blend, maybe with a little splash of hazelnut creamer. Hazelnut always reminds me of the holidays. We used to go to my sister's house for Thanksgiving, and she would always make this sweet potato casserole with the little marshmallows on top. The marshmallows would get perfectly toasted and brown...

Oh, goodness me. I've completely lost track of what I was saying. I'm so sorry, doctor. You were asking about me not settling down? Yes, it's just... like I said, I keep rushing from the garden to the center to the errands because I feel like if I actually stop, if I just sit down and rest, everything is just going to completely fall apart.

Oh, it's been this way my whole life. Even back in grade school, it was the same story. My teachers were always writing on my report cards that I was a bright girl but just so careless. Well, no... I don't think so. I can't really think of a time where I was so focused I didn't notice what was going on around me. Usually it's the exact opposite, like I was just saying. I notice everything. 

My husband, God rest his soul, he was the one who could do that. He would sit in his recliner, the brown leather one that we got from Sears... oh, they don't make furniture like that anymore. Solid wood frame. We had to wait six weeks for it to be delivered because it was a special order. The delivery men scuffed the doorframe bringing it in, and he was so upset. But anyway, he would sit in that chair and watch his war documentaries on the History Channel, and the house could be falling down around him and he wouldn't even blink. The grandchildren would be running around, screaming, playing tag right through the living room, and he'd just be staring at the television. The oldest one, Tommy, he's in college now, studying engineering. He always loved building things. When he was little, we bought him those plastic blocks, the ones you snap together... Legos! Yes, Legos. He built a whole city on the dining room table once. We had to eat off TV trays for a week because he wouldn't let us take it down. TV trays always make me think of those frozen dinners, the ones with the little brownie in the middle compartment...

Oh, I'm sorry. I'm doing it again, aren't I? But no, to answer your question, I don't really get hyper-focused like that. I'm usually too busy noticing every little thing to tune it all out.

Diagnosed? No, heavens no. Nobody ever said anything about that to me. Back when I was coming up, they didn't really have names for things like this, or at least they didn't use them on regular folks. If you couldn't sit still, they just called you a chatterbox or a daydreamer. 

Our family doctor back then was Dr. Higgins. He was a lovely man, always wore these thick tweed suits even in the dead of summer. His office was right above the old pharmacy on Main Street. You had to walk up this terribly steep flight of wooden stairs to get there, and they creaked so loudly. The pharmacy downstairs had a real soda fountain, though. After a checkup, my mother would let me get a cherry vanilla float. They used real maraschino cherries, the bright red ones, and the syrup would sink to the bottom of the tall glass. I bought a jar of those cherries just last week for my granddaughter's visit, but she wouldn't even touch them. Kids these days are so picky. She only wants to eat those little fruit snacks that come in the shiny pouches. They just taste like plastic to me, and they stick to your teeth terribly. I had a terrible time at the dentist last month because I ate a sticky caramel and it pulled a crown right off. Dr. Evans, my dentist now, he said I really need to be careful with chewy candies at my age, but my husband always used to keep a bowl of Werther's Originals on the coffee table...

Oh, my stars. Listen to me going on about cherries and dentists. I'm so sorry, doctor. I completely lost the thread again. But no, to answer your question, no doctor has ever told me I had that, and I've never taken any kind of treatment for it. This is really the first time anyone has ever asked me these sorts of questions.

It's like I don't take a real breath the entire day. \n\nSpeaking of papers, I was sorting through this big stack of mail yesterday and found a catalog for gardening supplies. Oh, absolutely. It's a real struggle. I can sit down with the senior center newsletter or a choir schedule, and I start out just fine. But after a few minutes, I realize my eyes have gone over the same lines three or four times, and I have absolutely no idea what I just read. 

It happened just yesterday with the newsletter. They were announcing the new schedule for the water aerobics class. I used to love water aerobics when Mary was still teaching it. She had this wonderful playlist with all these old Motown hits. We'd be doing our leg lifts to The Supremes. Mary moved down to Florida to be closer to her daughter, Susan. Susan just had a baby, a little girl. They named her Eleanor, which I think is just a lovely, classic name. Not like some of the names you hear nowadays. Focusing so much I lose track of time? Goodness, no. I don't think I've ever had that happen. It's usually the exact opposite for me. I can't stay on one thing for more than a few minutes before my mind is off somewhere else entirely. 

My husband, though, rest his soul, he was like that. He could spend hours in the garage working on his model trains. He had this whole elaborate setup that took up half the space in there. He'd paint these tiny little figures, the passengers and the conductors, with a brush that had maybe three bristles on it. I don't know how his eyes could take it. He used to buy his supplies at this little hobby shop downtown, right next to the old bakery. Oh, the smell of that bakery in the mornings! They made these wonderful bear claws with almond paste inside. We used to get them every Sunday after church. The baker, Mr. Rossi, he had this big white mustache that always seemed to have a dusting of powdered sugar on it. He was such a kind man. When my husband passed, Mr. Rossi brought over a whole tray of assorted pastries for the reception. It was so thoughtful, but of course, nobody was really eating much. The reception was at the church hall, the one with the terrible green carpeting. They really need to replace that carpet, it's been there since the late seventies, I think...

Oh, my. Listen to me. I'm so sorry, doctor. I'm off on another trip down memory lane. But no, to answer your question, I've never been able to focus on anything that intensely. I'm usually just bouncing from one thing to the next.

But yes, to answer your question, the restlessness and the trouble sitting still... it's been there since I was a little girl in school.\n\nDoctor: Do you often find yourself easily distracted by things around you, even when you're trying to focus on something?\n\nPatient: Oh, goodness, yes. All the time. It's so frustrating because I really do try to focus, especially when I'm sitting down at the kitchen table to sort through the bills and paperwork. My family set up this whole system for me, with colored folders and everything, but it just doesn't seem to help. \n\nJust the other day, I was sitting there, trying to figure out the electric bill, and I heard a car door slam outside. I had to get up and look out the window to see who it was. It was just the mail carrier, but then I saw that the Johnsons across the street had put out their Halloween decorations already. It's not even October! They have this giant inflatable pumpkin that lights up at night. It reminds me of the pumpkin patch we used to take the kids to when they were little. They had a hayride that went all the way around the farm, and you could pick your own apples, too. The Honeycrisp apples were always the best. I used to make a deep-dish apple pie with a crumble topping. My mother taught me how to make the crumble—it has to have just the right amount of cold butter cut into the flour and brown sugar. If the butter gets too warm, the crumble just turns into a greasy mess. I tried making it with margarine once when things were tight, but it just wasn't the same. Margarine never tastes quite right, does it? It always has that sort of artificial flavor...\n\nOh, dear me. I'm so sorry, doctor. I've done it again, haven't I? I just get so easily sidetracked. What was I saying? Oh, right, the distractions. Yes, it's terrible. Even if it's not a noise outside, if my phone just lights up silently, or if I even just have a sudden thought about what needs doing in the garden, I'm completely pulled off track. Before I know it, the bills are forgotten and I'm off doing something else entirely.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever find yourself so intensely focused on something that you tune out everything else around you?\n\nPatient: Well, no... I don't think so. I can't really think of a time where I was so focused I didn't notice what was going on around me. Usually it's the exact opposite, like I was just saying. I notice everything. \n\nMy husband, God rest his soul, he was the one who could do that. He would sit in his recliner, the brown leather one that we got from Sears... oh, they don't make furniture like that anymore. Solid wood frame. We had to wait six weeks for it to be delivered because it was a special order. The delivery men scuffed the doorframe bringing it in, and he was so upset. But anyway, he would sit in that chair and watch his war documentaries on the History Channel, and the house could be falling down around him and he wouldn't even blink. The grandchildren would be running around, screaming, playing tag right through the living room, and he'd just be staring at the television. The oldest one, Tommy, he's in college now, studying engineering. He always loved building things. When he was little, we bought him those plastic blocks, the ones you snap together... Legos! Yes, Legos. He built a whole city on the dining room table once. We had to eat off TV trays for a week because he wouldn't let us take it down. TV trays always make me think of those frozen dinners, the ones with the little brownie in the middle compartment...\n\nOh, I'm sorry. I'm doing it again, aren't I? But no, to answer your question, I don't really get hyper-focused like that. I'm usually too busy noticing every little thing to tune it all out.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever been diagnosed with or treated for ADHD?\n\nPatient: Diagnosed? No, heavens no. Nobody ever said anything about that to me. Back when I was coming up, they didn't really have names for things like this, or at least they didn't use them on regular folks. If you couldn't sit still, they just called you a chatterbox or a daydreamer. \n\nOur family doctor back then was Dr. Higgins. He was a lovely man, always wore these thick tweed suits even in the dead of summer. His office was right above the old pharmacy on Main Street. You had to walk up this terribly steep flight of wooden stairs to get there, and they creaked so loudly. The pharmacy downstairs had a real soda fountain, though. After a checkup, my mother would let me get a cherry vanilla float. They used real maraschino cherries, the bright red ones, and the syrup would sink to the bottom of the tall glass. I bought a jar of those cherries just last week for my granddaughter's visit, but she wouldn't even touch them. Kids these days are so picky. She only wants to eat those little fruit snacks that come in the shiny pouches. They just taste like plastic to me, and they stick to your teeth terribly. I had a terrible time at the dentist last month because I ate a sticky caramel and it pulled a crown right off. Dr. Evans, my dentist now, he said I really need to be careful with chewy candies at my age, but my husband always used to keep a bowl of Werther's Originals on the coffee table...\n\nOh, my stars. Listen to me going on about cherries and dentists. I'm so sorry, doctor. I completely lost the thread again. But no, to answer your question, no doctor has ever told me I had that, and I've never taken any kind of treatment for it. This is really the first time anyone has ever asked me these sorts of questions.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever had difficulty sustaining attention on tasks or activities, such as reading or conversations?\n\nPatient: Oh, absolutely. It's a real struggle. I can sit down with the senior center newsletter or a choir schedule, and I start out just fine. But after a few minutes, I realize my eyes have gone over the same lines three or four times, and I have absolutely no idea what I just read. \n\nIt happened just yesterday with the newsletter. They were announcing the new schedule for the water aerobics class. I used to love water aerobics when Mary was still teaching it. She had this wonderful playlist with all these old Motown hits. We'd be doing our leg lifts to The Supremes. Mary moved down to Florida to be closer to her daughter, Susan. Susan just had a baby, a little girl. They named her Eleanor, which I think is just a lovely, classic name. Not like some of the names you hear nowadays. My neighbor's grandson is named Jaxson, but they spell it with an 'x' and an 's'. I don't know how the poor boy is ever going to learn to write it in cursive. Do they even teach cursive in schools anymore? I remember spending hours with those lined workbooks, practicing my capital Qs. They always looked like a number 2 to me. I used a fountain pen that my father gave me for my 16th birthday. It had real blue ink that would stain your fingers if you weren't careful. He bought it at the stationary shop that used to be next to the old movie theater...\n\nOh, dear. I'm doing it again. I'm so sorry. But yes, reading is very hard. Conversations, too. I try to listen, I really do, but someone will be talking to me, and suddenly I'm thinking about whether I left the porch light on, and I haven't heard a word they've said for the last five minutes.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your difficulties with focus, organization, and restlessness have caused significant problems in your life for as long as you can remember?\n\nPatient: Oh, yes. Yes, I really do think so. It’s been this way for as long as I can remember, truly. Even back in grade school, my report cards always said the exact same thing. My teachers wrote that I was bright but careless. I was always losing my papers, talking out of turn, and they were constantly having to remind me to stay in my seat or just finish my work. \n\nI remember my third-grade teacher, Mrs. Gable, she was particularly strict about staying in your seat. She had this enormous beehive hairdo, just sprayed absolutely solid. You could smell the Aqua Net hairspray before she even walked into the classroom. My mother used to use that exact same hairspray. She’d buy it by the case at the beauty supply store down on 4th Street. That whole block is completely gone now, replaced by that big ugly concrete parking garage, but back then it was just so lively. We’d go to Woolworth's after she finished her shopping and sit at the lunch counter. I always got a grilled cheese sandwich and a cherry coke. The waitress there, Betty, she wore these little white aprons with ruffled edges that her sister made for her. Her sister was a wonderful seamstress, actually. She made my prom dress years later... it was this lovely seafoam green taffeta with a sweetheart neckline, and we had to drive all the way to the next town over just to find the right matching shoes...\n\nOh, dear me. I've wandered completely off the path again, haven't I? Seafoam green dresses... what on earth were we talking about? Oh, right, if it's been a problem my whole life. Yes, I'm afraid so. Ever since I was a little girl getting scolded by Mrs. Gable, it's just always been a struggle.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever found yourself so focused on an activity that you lost track of time and everything else around you?\n\nPatient: Focusing so much I lose track of time? Goodness, no. I don't think I've ever had that happen. It's usually the exact opposite for me. I can't stay on one thing for more than a few minutes before my mind is off somewhere else entirely. \n\nMy husband, though, rest his soul, he was like that. He could spend hours in the garage working on his model trains. He had this whole elaborate setup that took up half the space in there. He'd paint these tiny little figures, the passengers and the conductors, with a brush that had maybe three bristles on it. I don't know how his eyes could take it. He used to buy his supplies at this little hobby shop downtown, right next to the old bakery. Oh, the smell of that bakery in the mornings! They made these wonderful bear claws with almond paste inside. We used to get them every Sunday after church. The baker, Mr. Rossi, he had this big white mustache that always seemed to have a dusting of powdered sugar on it. He was such a kind man. When my husband passed, Mr. Rossi brought over a whole tray of assorted pastries for the reception. It was so thoughtful, but of course, nobody was really eating much. The reception was at the church hall, the one with the terrible green carpeting. They really need to replace that carpet, it's been there since the late seventies, I think...\n\nOh, my. Listen to me. I'm so sorry, doctor. I'm off on another trip down memory lane. But no, to answer your question, I've never been able to focus on anything that intensely. I'm usually just bouncing from one thing to the next.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever had a comprehensive evaluation for ADHD or taken any medication for symptoms of inattention or hyperactivity?\n\nPatient: An evaluation? Or medication? No, never. Goodness, when I was growing up, nobody even talked about things like that. You were just a daydreamer or a chatterbox, and that was that. I suppose they just expected you to grow out of it eventually. \n\nMy aunt Clara, she was a bit like me, always flitting about like a moth. She never sat still long enough to drink a full cup of tea before it went cold. She used to collect those little ceramic thimbles from all over the world. People would bring them back for her when they traveled. I remember she had one from Holland that looked like a tiny windmill, and the blades actually turned if you flicked them. She kept them all in this glass display cabinet in her front parlor. That parlor was always freezing, even in the middle of July. She had these heavy velvet curtains that she kept drawn because she said the sun would fade the upholstery on her settee. It was a beautiful settee, though, deep burgundy with carved wooden legs that looked like lion paws. My cousin Thomas accidentally chipped one of the paws with his toy truck when he was about five. He was always crashing those metal trucks into the baseboards. His mother bought them for him at the five-and-dime... they don't make toys like that anymore, do they? Now everything is plastic and takes batteries. The batteries cost more than the toy itself half the time. I tried to buy batteries for my kitchen clock last week, the one shaped like a teapot, and I stood in the aisle at the pharmacy for twenty minutes just staring at all the different sizes...\n\nOh, dear. I've done it again, haven't I? I am so sorry. You asked about medication or being tested. No, I've never done anything like that. This is the first time I've ever really talked to a doctor about it."
